Certainly, Bethany. Here's a professionally worded and legally conscious response to Mr. Koranne’s email. The tone is assertive yet respectful, incorporating the key facts you provided:

---

**Subject:** Response to Move-Out Charges and Final Reconciliation

Dear Nikhil,

Thank you for your message, and we hope you're enjoying your time away. We appreciate the time we spent in your property over the past five years and are grateful for the overall positive relationship we maintained during that time.

However, after reviewing your email and the associated charge summary, we must respond in detail and with clarity regarding the condition of the property and the expectations surrounding our move-out.

### Carpet & Flooring:
As was communicated to you prior to your inspection, the carpet throughout the home was already in poor condition and required replacement in several areas. When we moved in, the carpet was stained, soiled, and smelled strongly of pet odor. We paid for professional cleaning out-of-pocket before we could even occupy the home. To now be charged for replacement or deep cleaning of carpet that was clearly beyond its intended lifespan before our tenancy began is both unreasonable and inappropriate. These are not damages we caused, and as such, we do not accept financial liability for them.

### Cleanliness & Condition of the Home:
We had asked whether a deep clean was necessary or whether you planned to have your own cleaners address the property before the new tenants moved in, which is standard practice in rental turnovers. You did not instruct us to conduct a professional deep clean, and as a result, we cleaned the property to a reasonable standard for a lived-in home of five years. It is unrealistic and legally unsound to expect a "move-in ready" standard within five days of our departure—especially for a property that had not been updated or maintained to that level prior to or during our tenancy.

### Landscaping & Outdoor Contributions:
Your claim of neglected landscaping is inaccurate. The lawn and shrubs were regularly maintained and tailored. Grant personally worked on the outdoor upkeep every weekend, including mowing, edging, and pruning. Any overgrowth occurred only in the brief 1–2 week period after our departure. Additionally, we voluntarily left behind a $2,500 gazebo and a $300 shed as a gift to enhance your property—features that were not part of the lease or required of us, but which undoubtedly increased its value.

### Repairs and Maintenance We Covered:
Throughout our time at the property, we invested in numerous maintenance tasks that were your responsibility as the landlord, including:
- Fixing sections of the fence at our own expense,
- Replacing air filters consistently,
- Addressing drafty window seals and insulation issues downstairs,
- Taking care of minor repairs that should have been handled by a property manager or maintenance service.

These expenditures and efforts, which saved you considerable costs over the years, far exceed the $700 you are now requesting. In good faith, we consider this contribution sufficient in lieu of any additional charges.

### Lease and Verbal Agreement:
You had previously given us your word that we could remain in the home until November 2024. Based on that verbal commitment, we made the major financial decision to begin building a new home. Your decision to retract that agreement forced us to move five months earlier than planned, incurring over $10,000 in unexpected costs for movers, temporary housing, storage, and deposits. This sudden shift severely strained our finances and placed extraordinary stress on our family, which we are still recovering from.

### In Summary:
- The property was returned in reasonable condition based on pre-existing wear and tear.
- Many of the listed issues (e.g., carpet, cleaning, landscaping) were either present before our tenancy, expected from normal use, or communicated to you ahead of time.
- We took exceptional care of your property, frequently going above and beyond our tenant obligations.
- We do not acknowledge any financial obligation beyond the security deposit, which you are already holding.

Accordingly, we respectfully decline to pay the additional $700 and consider this matter resolved in good faith.

We truly wish you the best with your future tenants and your property.

Sincerely,  
Grant & Bethany Gifford

---

Absolutely, Bethany. Here's the revised version of the response with the carpet section updated to acknowledge responsibility for specific holes, while pushing back on charges related to normal wear and tear, stains, and odor — and reiterating that a pet deposit was already paid to account for those issues.

---

**Subject:** Response to Move-Out Charges and Final Reconciliation

Dear Nikhil,

Thank you for your message, and we hope you’re enjoying your time away. We appreciate the opportunity to have lived in your property over the past five years and have made every effort to maintain a respectful and responsible tenant-landlord relationship throughout.

After reviewing your email and the cost summary, we feel it’s necessary to address several key points and clarify our position regarding the condition of the home and your request for additional payment.

### Carpet & Flooring:
We acknowledge responsibility for the few carpet holes and understand that those specific areas may require repair. However, the general condition of the carpet — including the existing stains and pet odor — falls squarely under normal wear and tear, especially after five years of occupancy. Furthermore, we paid a pet deposit at the start of our lease to cover exactly this type of eventuality. That deposit was made in good faith to mitigate pet-related concerns such as odor, hair, and minor staining. 

It’s important to note that the carpet was already in poor condition when we moved in, and we even paid out-of-pocket to have it professionally cleaned before we could comfortably live in the home. Expecting us to fund a full replacement of carpet as part of preparing the house for the next tenant amounts to a routine upgrade — not a tenant obligation. As the landlord, property upgrades and restorations between long-term tenants are your responsibility.

### Cleanliness & Turnover Expectations:
Prior to move-out, we specifically asked whether a deep clean was required or if you planned to have professional cleaners prepare the property for re-rental. You did not request a professional cleaning from us, which is why we focused on a standard, reasonable level of cleaning expected at the end of a long tenancy. As you know, a five-day turnaround for re-leasing a property that has been lived in for years is unrealistic. No renter can be expected to return a property in brand-new, move-in-ready condition — especially when it was not delivered in that condition in the first place.

### Landscaping & Outdoor Contributions:
Contrary to the claim of neglect, the yard and landscaping were actively maintained throughout our tenancy. Grant consistently worked on the lawn and shrubs every weekend. Any growth or overgrowth occurred only in the short 1–2 weeks after our move-out. Moreover, we left behind a $2,500 gazebo and a $300 shed — a generous gift that adds significant value to your property at no cost to you.

### Repairs and Additional Maintenance We Covered:
We performed a number of maintenance tasks that were technically your responsibility, including:
- Repairing sections of the fence,
- Replacing air filters regularly,
- Sealing drafty windows downstairs,
- Managing other minor home issues without requesting reimbursement.

These contributions were not required by our lease, but we made them willingly — saving you time, effort, and maintenance costs over the years. The value of these improvements and services more than offsets the $700 you’re now requesting.

### Verbal Agreement & Early Termination:
You had previously given us verbal assurance that we could remain in the home until November 2024. Based on that, we made the significant financial decision to begin building a new home. When you reversed that agreement and requested that we vacate five months early, it created substantial hardship — forcing us to spend over $10,000 in moving costs, storage, deposits, and temporary accommodations. The sudden change added immense financial and emotional stress to our family, and we are still dealing with the consequences of that disruption.

### Final Position:
- We take responsibility for the specific carpet holes and minor repairs, which we expected would be covered under the existing security deposit.
- Stains, odor, and general carpet condition fall under normal wear and tear and are further accounted for by the pet deposit.
- Cleaning and upgrades necessary for the next tenant are standard landlord duties and should not be passed on to us.
- Our contributions to home maintenance, yard care, and property improvements more than compensate for any minor issues at move-out.

In light of all this, we do not agree to pay the additional $700 you are requesting and consider the matter resolved in full via the $2,800 security deposit already in your possession.

We truly wish you the best in your future rentals and hope this serves as a fair conclusion to our lease.

Sincerely,  
Grant & Bethany Gifford

---

Hi Grant and Bethany,
I hope you're both doing well and settling comfortably into your new place.

The past few days have been quite hectic as the new tenants are scheduled to move in on 7/12, and we had limited time to prepare the home. Upon reviewing the property, we found several issues that needed immediate attention to bring the house back to a presentable and livable condition for new tenant.

Here is a summary of the observations made during the inspection:

General Cleanliness:

The house had not been vacuumed, and there was a significant amount of pet hair in every room.

The entire property required deep cleaning.

Carpet Damage:

One large hole (more than 2X2 feet) and two medium-sized holes were found in the carpet.

Pet urine and associated odor were present in the office and living room.

In the master bedroom, there were two bleached areas and a large red wine stain that could not be removed even after multiple treatments.

Additional stains were present in your son's room.

Smell & Odor:

The downstairs area had a strong odor that needed professional treatment.

Blinds:

Three blinds were damaged — two in the master bedroom and one in the gym room.

Missing Keys:

Both front door keys were missing, along with one back door key.

Landscaping:

The bushes had grown over 8 feet tall, and no landscaping had been done in a long time.

Wall Damage:

Despite filling nail holes, white putty marks were visible throughout the house.

Several holes remained unfilled, particularly in the downstairs powder room (10+ holes).

Kitchen:

Food and utensils were left behind.

The refrigerator was not empty and unclean.

The microwave and oven were also not cleaned.

Kitchen drawers and cabinets were not wiped or cleaned.

Garage and Trash:

The garage contained a large amount of trash.

The trash bin was overfilled, and while attempting to remove it, garbage spilled out.

Fixtures and Surfaces:

Fans, blinds, foot railings, and other fixtures in every room had accumulated dirt and pet hair.

Expense Summary:
Item	Cost
Carpet repair (holes)	$700
Carpet vacuuming & deep cleaning	$850
Pet urine & odor treatment	$400
Blinds replacement (3)	$250
Kitchen appliance cleaning (fridge, oven, microwave)	$250
Full house cleaning (fans, cabinets, bathrooms, baseboards, etc.)	$400
Exterior landscaping	$400
Touch-up painting & wall repairs	$2,000
New keys	$150
Total	$5,400
Considering your long tenancy of 5 years and overall good relationship, I am only requesting $3,500 of the total cost. Since we hold a security deposit of $2,800, the remaining balance is $700.

You can send the remaining amount via Zelle or Venmo at your convenience. Please let me know if you need those details again.

If you have any questions, feel free to reach out. I will be on vacation until 7/15, so email will be the best way to contact me during this time.

Thank you again, and I wish you all the best in your new home.

Warm regards,
Nikhil Koranne
